blocks.text: The scene is a section of a parlor car speeding toward New York, and not so very far from it when the curtain rises. We see only two chairs clearly; the ends of the car dissolve in shadows. On these less visible chairs are tossed vague overcoats and magazines; the racks above them are filled with baggage. There is a bag or two overhead; on the floor are quantities of Sunday newspapers, along with plenty of rotogravure sections, curling carelessly against the bottoms of the chairs. It is night, and the shades are down.

In the two vital chairs sit a boy and a girl. The name of the boy, as we presently find out, is Fred Stevens. The girl is Edna Baker. She sits with her back to him, and is absorbed in a magazine when the curtain goes up. The boy, who is not exactly a literary type, is a bit restless. He wriggles in his seat, sighs, peers discreetly at the girl, who pays no attention. With a bit too much of a flourish, as though he thus hoped to attract her attention, he whips out a time table and studies it. Consults his watch; swings and peers out of the window, hand cupped over eyes to exclude the light. Then he swings back, relaxes﻿—and looks toward the girl again. She swings her chair around for a second; peers down the aisle, but swings back without having permitted the boy to catch her eye. He rattles his newspaper a trifle obviously; indulges in a bit of bad whistling; hums a little. She swings around again; another look down the aisle. Fred girds up his courage to break the ice. The girl, who has the situation well in hand, gives sudden and demure attention to an imaginary spot on her dress. She chips at it with a fingernail.
Ever so properly, in the manner of a young woman who never has been spoken to on a train before.
By turning away from him again she indicates that she is not encouraging a continuation of the interview.
I thought maybe you might want to read.
She gives him a small smile.
Trying desperately to keep things going.
You got on at Hudson, didn’t you?
A pause after this momentous remark.
Feeling that it’s all right to help along.
She’s in New York now, or at least she was the last time I heard of her. Working at Saks’. Grace Crowell.
I used to know a Mildred Crowell, but her name wasn’t Grace.
Mildred Crowell’s brother was quite a billiard player. Three cushions. Eddie, his name was.
He comes back to vital matters.

It’s funny how we lose track of people. Some of the girls I used to go with, they still live there yet, but I never look any of them up, except Gertie Hutton. I guess it’s terrible of me not to, because if a person’s got good friends, they ought to keep them.
He has finally managed to bring that up.
I had to be. It was me they give it for. I mean, I was the guest of honor.
He indicates a shining yellow suitcase at his side.
I like a man to have a middle name. Girls don’t usually have them. I’m just plain Edna.
You know how to make pretty speeches.
I bet you’re used to them.
There’s another one. I’m not so used to them that I don’t like to hear them, especially from people whom I think they’re sincere.
I don’t say things unless I mean them.
Talking about speeches, you ought to heard the speech Carl Williams, made when he give me this bag. At the banquet, I mean. I guess I blushed, the things he said about me. A lot more than I deserve.
I bet they were sorry to see you go. You look like the kind of a man men would like. And girls, too.
I don’t go around much with girls.
I don’t go much with men, either.
A pause; that subject’s cleaned up.

My brother always insists on me riding in it. He says the day coach is generally dirty, for one thing﻿—and another thing, the men that ride in the day coach are the kind that try and make up to pretty girls. That sounds like I was throwing a bouquet at myself, but I’m just repeating what Dick said. That’s my brother’s name, Dick. I guess a brother always thinks their sister is good-looking.
I believe in a man sticking up for their sister, or any woman. I got no use for a man that don’t respect woman’s hood. Where would a man be if it wasn’t for their mothers and sisters and wives?
I haven’t got one myself﻿—yet. I ain’t been lucky enough to meet a woman who would be a good pal as well as a sweetheart. I want my wife to be like mother used to be.
I love to have a man love their mother.
I wished mine was still here. Like Carl Williams said in his speech last night﻿—if she was still here, maybe she would be a little proud of me.

He made quite a speech, all right. He said the boys expected me to make Irving Berlin jealous. I said I didn’t want to make nobody jealous, but I wanted to make my friends proud. I said my only regret in going to New York was on account of leaving so many good friends behind, and as soon as my songs begun to sell up in the hundred thousands, and my dreams came true, I would invite them all down to visit me on Broadway and show them the sights.
It must be wonderful to have a gift like that.
That’s what Benny Davis called it﻿—a gift. I guess you’ve heard of him﻿—he’s turned out a hundred smash hits.
Oh, How I Miss You Tonight!
He sings a strain of it.
Are you going to be partners with him?

If he wants me to, and I guess he will when I show him Benny Davis’s letter. That’s the hard part, getting acquainted. I’d have broke away a long while ago only for my sister. I couldn’t leave her alone.
She’ll miss you just the same. I know how sisters feel, especially when their brother is like you or Dick.
Well, anyway, she got married, and I give them a pair of bookends.
Dives for his bag and starts opening it.
I’ll bet it would cost more than that.
Marion can sew, all right. My mother used to say she was a born seamstress.
It’s too bad you’re not my brother and I’d embroider your whole initials.
You don’t have to be a man’s sister to embroider their shirt.
You don’t need to be scared of me, girlie. I treat all women like they was my sister. Till I find out different.
He’d keep his distance if I was around.
I got plenty of excuses for being there. I got a cavity as big as the Grand Canyon.
Laughing a little harder than is necessary.
He’ll fix it for you. He’s a wonderful dentist.
If I come, it’ll probably be when he’s out to lunch.
Then what would you come for?
I’d rather you told me. I’m a bad guesser.
I might come to see you. Would you let me?
I’d love it, if you wanted to.
I wouldn’t say so if I didn’t.
No, I won’t. Your smile will always haunt me.
I’ll bet you’re a wonderful songwriter. No wonder your friends gave you that big dinner.
It certainly was quite a banquet. I bet some of my pals got a headache today, all right.
I hope you haven’t got one.
No. Liquor don’t afflict me like most people.
I hardly ever touch it myself, only once in a great while, at a party.
Girls ought to lay off it entirely.
Take some of those women in Schenectady and they want to go out somewhere every night and guzzle. Married women, too.
I don’t see how they can, with a home to take care of.
Either they get all dressed up and drag their husband to a dance or a card party every night, or either they lay around the house in a wrapper.
When I marry I’ll be just as careful of my appearance as I am now. I believe a husband appreciates a wife dressing up for him.

The man I marry won’t have any complaints. I make practically all my own clothes. Caroline﻿—she’s the girl I used to live with﻿—she used to say I always looked like I had just stepped out of a bandbox, even if we were only sitting in our room. We hardly ever went out evenings; personally I prefer to stay home and read, or else just sit and dream. But still I always bathe and change my clothes even when I’m only going to cook dinner.
I think I’ll take a room with a bathroom when I get to the hotel.
Where are you going to stay?

The Hotel Somerset. They got rooms with a bathroom right in the room, so you don’t have to go out of the room. And it’s close to the music publishing houses and the Friars’ Club﻿—any place I want to go, I can walk. Except to Paul Sears’ place. He probably lives in some swell apartment, or maybe a country place in Great Neck or Jamaica.
A successful man like he wouldn’t live in Jamaica.

Well, some place. I don’t know much about New York; I only been there once before, with Carl Williams. He’s the fella that made the speech last night. It was the first time he’s been away from home in the evening since he was married. He’s got a wife and baby now.

It’s nothing against a woman to like babies. Carl’s wife certainly likes hers. She’s made him a nice home, too. He didn’t have to buy hardly anything in the way of furniture; her grandmother gave her a bedroom suit and she bought some herself with money she saved while she was working at Berger’s.

She must be a good deal like myself. I could almost start housekeeping with the things I’ve got. I suppose I’m silly and old-fashioned, but I always thought a girl should bring her husband something besides herself. I even wouldn’t mind going on working after I was married, till my husband established himself.
The girl I marry won’t never have to work. I don’t believe God ever meant for a woman to endure a life of druggery.
It’s been a shorter trip than usual, for some reason.
Trying to peer out the window.
If we was on the other side we could see the Hudson River.
I know, but June and moon go together. They rhyme. I’m always thinking of words that rhyme, even when I ain’t working.
Yes, you could get other words to go with it. Spoon, and croon, and soon. Marry soon, or something.
Yeah. I wish I had some. I’m hungry.
You won’t be telling the truth, because I’m going to see you again.
You say that now. But you’ll forget all about me.
No, I won’t. Are you going right home when we get in?
I thought I’d go and get something to eat some place, only I wouldn’t know where to go if I didn’t have somebody with me that knowed where to go.
I can tell you a place where I go once in a while, the Little Venice. Though most of the time I stay home and cook my own dinner, just because I love to cook.
It’ll be a little late to cook tonight. I was wondering if you wouldn’t go along to this place, and maybe we could eat together.
It ain’t a very expensive place, is it?
Oh, no. The last time I went, there was two of us and we had hot roast beef sandwiches, and peas, and coffee, and it only came to a dollar-twenty.

The scene is one of those Riverside Drive apartments, in a place called New York City. It is up in the neighborhood of One Hundred and Sixteenth Street, and once it was pretty good. It’s a bit run down now, and since people began moving to the East Side the neighborhood has become somewhat déclassé﻿—not more so, however, than Paul Sears, the tenant of this particular apartment.
We see the living-room, if you can call it living. There is a piano, because Paul Sears is a composer. The rest of the furniture is what you might imagine, or worse.

Paul, a commonplace-looking man in his middle thirties, is at the piano when the curtain rises. He is in his shirt sleeves and is alternately hitting a few discouraged keys and making probably meaningless notations on the music sheet in front of him. He lacks one finger of being a two-fingered piano player. He is laboriously going over the same phrase again and again. And if you had never even heard it once, it would be too often.

Lucille, his wife, comes on from the rear rooms of the apartment. A spare but still attractive woman, on whom three years of marriage with Paul Sears have left their mark. She looks around for something. Finds it. It turns out to be a copy of the Graphic. She drops listlessly into a chair and starts to read. Paul continues torturing the piano.
I read it. Automobile man. Probably drives a truck.
If he does, at least she’ll have something to go places in.
I got Myra her first job; I introduced her to Dillingham.
Ask the doorman down at the Globe. He used to have to carry her in.
She never took a drink when I knew her.
Starts hitting the same old notes.
Why don’t you go out? You could go out if you want to.
You know she’s got a date with Hart. I suppose you want me trailing along.
I don’t expect you to take me anywhere, except maybe for a walk around the block. That’s free.
I don’t enjoy laying around here no more than you do. I’m not a nun.
That’s the first I’ve heard about it.
You wait till this number gets over. We’ll go everywhere then.
I can play as good as I need to. I can play as good as Berlin, and he’s turned out twice as many hits as anybody.
He knows what people want. He appeals to the women.
It ruins a composer to play the piano too good. They depend on fancy harmony and tempo, instead of pretty melodies.
His eye drawn to the newspaper.
He’s pretty pleased about it, too.
At least he won’t starve to death.
It was me that was responsible for Gershwin getting his start. I brought him and Georgie White together.
Because I don’t want him to come in the office yet, that’s why. I’m keeping him under cover till I get rid of Fagan.
If there’s one thing that’ll round out my day, it’s entertaining a lyric-writer.

This fella ain’t like the rest of them. He’s got a fresh slant. Take fellas like Fagan, that’s been around Broadway all their life, and all their lyrics sound just alike. If Fagan gave me a new idea, I’d drop dead. But this fella’s got a fresh slant.
Fagan would drop even deader if you gave him a new tune.
That’s so long ago I don’t see how you remember it.
Old man Goebel remembers it, and so does Hart. They made enough money out of it.
Yes, they do! There’s plenty fellas around the club that’s just as flat as I am.
I’ll tell you who’s got money, if you want to know, and that’s Stevens.
This lyric-writer, Stevens. He’s got money.
A lot of good that’ll do me.
His eye falls on his watch.
What about him and her, anyway? If she’s engaged to him, aren’t they ever going to get married?
You’ll know as soon as there’s anything to know.
He’ll wriggle off the hook some way. If you ask me he’s getting tired of her already.
Just the luck I’m running in. If I ever marry again, it’ll be a woman without a sister.
She don’t cost you much, and she’s company for me.
Yeah. You ought to be able to place her, with your influence.
At the telephone. Hello.﻿ ﻿… Oh, hello, Maxie!

There enters, from the rear rooms, Eileen. She has been drawn by the ring of the telephone, and comes on eagerly, expectantly. She is a young woman in her late twenties, and has plenty of good old-fashioned sex appeal. But with it she is a bit hard, a trifle worldly. She wears a good-looking and rather revealing negligee, and is carrying what seems to be an evening dress, on which she has been sewing, or trying to sew. She stops short as she senses that the phone call is not for her; relaxes. From her mouth comes a cloud of cigarette smoke. Paul, of course, has kept right on with his phone conversation.
Sure﻿—going to be here all evening.﻿ ﻿… All right.﻿ ﻿… Fine! He hangs up; turns to Lucille. Maxie’s coming over. Wait till you hear him play it﻿—a gesture toward his music﻿—then you’ll see!
I’ll go crazy, waiting around here!
Paul was trying to tell me he got her her first job; introduced her to Dillingham.
Oh, sure. He introduced Rogers to Peet, didn’t he?
Why don’t you look around Monday? See what you can find. Maybe I will. I’m lazy, I guess.
I’ve just been putting it off.
I’d never be too lazy to shop, if I had anything to shop with.
You wait till this number gets over.
Why don’t you try writing articles? They might be pretty near as good as your tunes.
You don’t have to worry about my tunes. Anyhow, I was talking to Lucille.
It’s time you did something more for Lucille besides talk to her!
If I was in your place, I’d keep pretty still in this house. That is, unless I was paying board.
It’s a good battle, by this time.
Only for your meals and a place to sleep!
You wouldn’t even have a job if it wasn’t for me! Do you think Hart is keeping you on the staff because you wrote a hit three years ago?
Well, make him lay off me, if he knows what’s good for him. If he keeps riding me, he’ll be looking for a new job!
Harms wouldn’t let you in their elevator!
As he goes proudly into the next room.

I wouldn’t mind waiting if there was something to wait for. I nearly go out of my mind, just sitting. You hear women brag about the nice, cozy evenings they spend at home with their husband. They’re not married to a piano tuner with ten thumbs.
What time was he going to call up?
Six o’clock. He said he’d call me the minute he got in. Maybe the train was late.
They aren’t late very often, from Philadelphia.

Of course, you know him better than I do, but when a man’s really crazy about a girl, he calls her up, I don’t care what he’s doing. It’s only when he begins cooling off that he finds excuses, like being in Philadelphia.
I know, but they’ve got phones there now, too.

If you think he’s cooling off you’re crazy! He’s insanely jealous. When I told him I was thinking of going out with Bert Livingston he was sore as hell. He said, “All right, go ahead and go out with him.” I asked him if he meant it, and he said, “Sure! Go out with the whole Lambs Club!” He’s insanely jealous and tries to hide it.
I’d go out with the janitor if he asked me. God, I’m sick of this place!
Why don’t you go to a picture?
You would, too, if Paul was any good.
I wonder what it’d be like if we’d stayed in Stroudsburg. I’d probably be married to Will Broderick, and we’d have a car﻿—
To drive over to Scranton in.
You’re a fool if you keep it up. You ought to break away while there’s still time.
That’s an easy thing to say. I haven’t got any grounds, in the first place.
You wouldn’t need grounds. Just get him up in court and let the judge look at him.
And even if I did get free, where am I? I’m not young any more. No man under sixty would look at me.
Well, men over sixty are more liable to have money than boy scouts.
Who does? Just the same, they’ve got their good points. They sleep eighteen hours a day. And they’re like little kids-they believe everything you tell them.
I never could fool anybody. That’s why I’ve been afraid to try anything, with Paul. He knows when I’m lying to him, every time.
Him! He isn’t even listening to you! You could have callers right in this room and he wouldn’t hear them come in﻿—not with all those God-given melodies ringing in his ears.
What’s the use of talking about it? There haven’t been any volunteers. Women can’t go wrong if they’re not invited.
All I can say is, if you don’t break away from him, you’re crazy!
And if I did, do you know what would happen? He’d write ten smash hits in a week. That’s my luck.﻿ ﻿… God! It would be wonderful to have some clothes and hold up my head again!
I’m through arguing with you. You’re hopeless.
Don’t you worry about me! If he wasn’t crazy about me, why would he be so insanely jealous? He’s insanely jealous!
Has he ever said anything halfway definite? About marrying, I mean?
What did he say it in?
He must be thinking of it. He doesn’t ever go out with anybody else.
Yeah﻿—about. He’s got to go to Chicago, and﻿—a lot of places.
What are you going to do with yourself all that time﻿—just sit around?
Maybe he’ll treat us to some shows﻿—I’ll ask him tonight. Maybe he’ll get us seats for some shows.
Do they still have seats at shows?
Disappearing into the hallway, talking as she goes.
He is a man in his late forties, easygoing, kindly. Wears a dinner coat. He is an arranger for Goebel’s, and he knows the popular song business backwards.
Well! All staying home on a Saturday night?
All nights are alike up here.
You didn’t come right up from the office, did you?
Go ahead, Maxie. She don’t know anything.
Think of me slaving down at the Orchard while you people enjoy all the comforts of home.
It certainly was a tough day for me when Edison invented the piano. Fixing up other people’s tunes﻿—there’s a life work for you.
His fingers rambling over the keys.
About to start, but resumes talking instead.
Thank God he can’t get that in a lyric.
He had the phone number, but he didn’t know the address.
How’d he get the phone number?
She shakes her head﻿—it’s too much for her.
What does he do﻿—write about counties instead of states?
I’ve been thinking maybe he and I could do something together, if I can get rid of Fagan.
Are you going to play it? Maxie plunges into the preliminary chords; Paul comes to life and sets himself to sing. Raises a warning finger in the direction of Lucille. Now listen!
“Golden West that seems so far away, Golden girl for whom I’m always pining, Don’t you know I love you night and day, But chiefly when the full bright moon is shining!”
He takes new breath for the chorus. Lucille, meanwhile, is listening intently, but hardly enthusiastically. In fact, you might almost think she didn’t like it so much.
“Montana moonlight, As bright as noon light, Oh, may it soon light My way to you! I know you’re lonely, My one and only, For I am lonely, Yes, lonely, too.”
At this point Lucille simply goes back to her sewing. Paul’s tone grows sharper as he sings, and she resigns herself to further listening.
“My heart is yearning. For kisses burning, For lips as sweet as a rose in June. I’m always dreaming. Of your eyes gleaming, Beneath the beaming. Montana Moon!”
Maxie plunges into a second chorus as Paul presses Lucille for an opinion. Don’t it sound great? The way Maxie plays it?
You don’t get Berlin’s songs to dance to. You get them to cry to.
All right. You can cry to this, too. “My heart is yearning for kisses burning.” That’s sad.

Do you want to know why? Because he gets a little sympathy now and then! He’s appreciated at home! He don’t sit around here night after night with you yapping your head off at him, telling him he’s all through!
Now, now! You’re going to write plenty of hits.
I’m trying to help you, not hurt you.
She doesn’t mean anything. Of course she wants to help you. But this number﻿—I wouldn’t count on it too much if I were you.
I just wouldn’t﻿—that’s all. You can’t tell which way they’re going to jump these days.
They’ll snap this one up. Unless they’re crazy.
Huh? I said Hart and Goebel were talking about Paul’s new number.
What did they say about it?
You mean they were talking about it today?
That don’t matter. What did they say about the song?
Listen﻿—what did they do? Turn it down?
They asked me, so there was nothing for me to do but give it to them. I had Nate sing it.
It’s the lyric kills it! The melody’s sure fire! Even if it don’t sell over the counter it’d get a good mechanical break.
He drops into a chair, discouraged.
You mustn’t let it worry you. The next one’ll be great, and you’ll forget all about this.
What else did they say﻿—when they heard it? Anything about me?
What could they say about you?
Maybe he’s just what you need. Maybe he’ll make all the difference in the world.
He is playing the piano again.
Playing with one hand and shaking hands with the other.
Paul tells me you’re a songwriter yourself.
Well, that’s all Paul needs﻿—that and the music.
I’m anxious to get started, all right. Since I got to town, all I’ve done so far is spend money.
Thanks. I guess I’m a little late. I got off the wrong subway station and there was an old woman there selling papers, and I stopped and talked to her because I knew she must be somebody’s mother.
I was right too, because she told me she has six sons. I feel sorry for old women that has to earn their living.
What do the boys do﻿—rent her the stand?
No, most of them are in a hospital and two of them had their foot cut off. She told me all about it and I give her a dollar.
You want to be careful in a place like New York. There’s all kinds of people waiting to take your money away from you.
I go there a lot﻿—just for the trip.
I seen the Goddest of Liberty, too﻿—I mean the statue. It cost a million dollars and weighs 225 ton.
He indulges in a fancy run.
Not for a minute giving up.
I’ve been waiting for somebody to go with.
And a red one when her husband’s home.

I was thinking of another idea on the way up here. Maybe a song about the melting pots﻿—all the immigrants from overseas who’ve come to the Land of Liberty. Take the Jews﻿—do you know there’s nearly two million Jews in New York City alone?
And then there’s the Hall of Fame, up to Washington Heights. They got everybody up there. Washington, Lincoln, Longfellow. They got two dozen﻿—what do you call ’em﻿—busts?
No. A man’s got to be dead for twenty-five years.
Wait! I want Stevens to show you one of his lyrics﻿—have you got that one with you? About the game?
I’ve got to be downtown at ten.
Here’s the verse. Are you ready?

“I don’t know why some people cry When things appear to go wrong; I always say ‘Laugh and be gay!’ Things cannot always go wrong! No use to pine, no use to whine, Things will come right if you just give them time.”
“Life is a game; we are but players﻿—”
Hey, bring it here! Maybe we can put some music to it.
I’ll see if I know any.

“Life is a game; we are but players Playing the best we know how. If you are beat, don’t let it wrangle; No one can win all the time. Sometimes the odds seem dead against you; What has to be, has to be, But smile just the same, for life is a game, And God is a fine referee.”

Maxie picks up the last line and sings it again, tacking on a rousing musical finale to fit. It is really the finish of “All Those Endearing Young Charms,” but so far as Fred is concerned it has been composed especially for his lyric. He is beaming with pleasure.
I haven’t got the second verse yet.
I like a song with love interest.
It’s just a title. You told me you’d rather have just a title and then write the tune first.

No, no. The verse will be about a fella that’s met a girl in June, when there was a moon shining, and then something happened so that she went away, or maybe he went away, and then whenever he looks up at the moon after that, he thinks of her. In the second verse, she’ll be doing the same thing for him.
He comes out strong on the “spoon”﻿—that’s right, anyhow.
To say that the lady is sarcastic is putting it mildly.
“Goodbye, everybody! I’m due at the Orchard! Glad to have met you, Stevens,”
Her tone indicates that this is the body blow.
She gives a broad wave of the hand, as if to say, “And if you want him, he’s yours.”
I’m glad to meet you, Miss Fletcher.
Oh, yes. Have you been in New York long?
Just a couple of weeks. I’m from Schenectady.
With the air of a person who is washing that up.
I was with the General Electric Company, but I left them.

Yes, I like it fine, but it costs money to live here. For instance, I had breakfast in the hotel this morning and it was ninety cents for salt mackerel and mashed potatoes and a cup of Instant Postum.
No wonder you think New York’s expensive! A few more breakfasts like that and you won’t have any money left.
I seen the Goddest of Liberty.
Oh, I mean the night places!
What do you say, Eileen? How about it?
Thinking hard; her eyes go involuntarily to the telephone.
Well, wait! It’d be great to go, all right, only the trouble is I got another engagement!
Oh, but you could put that off!
It ain’t that I don’t want to, but﻿—
You know, you really ought to. Paul was just saying that what you needed was to go places where they do the latest numbers and hear what kind of songs are getting over! That’s true, isn’t it, Paul?
Of course it is! Are we all set?
Well, I want to go all right. It’s only I don’t know on account of this other engagement.
So close to him that he is groggy.
We’ll go where we don’t have to dress.
How about the Orchard? Wouldn’t Maxie be surprised to see the four of us stroll in?
Well, wait a minute! It’s just that I didnt happen to bring much money with me﻿—
As long as you’re going to be partners!
Is that all right with you?
Does she live here with you all the time?
She’s a regular New York girlie.
Maybe it wouldn’t be a bad notion for you to knock around a few nights﻿—I mean, before we start working. Might give you some ideas.
Say, can I use your phone a minute?
Sure. Do you want the book?
I’d better clean up a bit.
Look! They was talking about this Orchard. That ain’t one of them expensive places, is it?
But I don’t-hello.﻿ ﻿… Hello.﻿ ﻿… Eddie?﻿ ﻿… I want to tell you something.
You seem to be having your troubles.
No, that wasn’t anything. Just a﻿—friend of mine.
It isn’t anybody. Just a little girl I happened to meet.
She’s just a﻿—a girl from a little town.
Listen﻿—it’s kind of early for the Orchard anyhow. So why don’t we take in the second show at the Capitol?
They’ve got a wonderful tap dancer up there! Better than Bill Robinson!
But say, the Cotton Club don’t get hot till three!
Who has never heard of that hour.
Oh, that’s all right! We can go to the Madrid or Richman’s in between!
But say, Richman’s burned down the other night!
I get dizzy if I climb a ladder!
